title: Decrypting Flume Water Monitor Traffic
excerpt: In my previous post, I tore apart a Flume water monitor and traced its communication path from the sensor, through the bridge, and up to Flume’s cloud MQTT server. I identified the encryption library (LibHydrogen), extracted a firmware ELF, and even managed to coerce the bridge into sending plaintext by corrupting the public key in flash. But that approach was destructive; the bridge couldn’t complete its handshake with Flume’s server, so real data stopped flowing.
content_html:
In my previous post, I tore apart a Flume water monitor and traced its communication path from the sensor, through the bridge, and up to Flume’s cloud MQTT server. I identified the encryption library (LibHydrogen), extracted a firmware ELF, and even managed to coerce the bridge into sending plaintext by corrupting the public key in flash. But that approach was destructive; the bridge couldn’t complete its handshake with Flume’s server, so real data stopped flowing.

Thinking I had reached a dead end, only to find another path turned out to be a pretty common occurrence for me. More and more thoughts on what I could have done differently, and what further research I could have done kept coming to me. And so I set out to continue to pursue my unhealthy obsession of figuring out exactly how I can read this data on the network.

Why I Thought This Would Be Harder

The firmware contains a full LibHydrogen Noise N key exchange implementation. In the disassembly, hydro_kx_n_1 lives at 0x4023382c (client side) and flume_kx_init_client at 0x40234550 calls it with PSK=NULL and the server’s public key loaded from flash. These functions have real cross-references to session key storage locations. Everything pointed to the bridge negotiating ephemeral session keys with Flume’s server, which would have made passive decryption impossible without writing a custom key pair to flash and implementing the full key exchange in the relay. I actually did do this and hoped to see it working, only to face yet another disappointment.

From the previous investigation, when I invalidated the magic prefix on the key storage area, Flume’s server responded with error 174: “Phydro crypto key exchange function failed.” That error message, combined with the key exchange code in the firmware, made it seem certain that session keys were in play.

But when I actually captured live traffic and tried decrypting with just the static device key, everything decrypted cleanly. No session keys involved. I’m sure I tried this last time, but I must not have had all secretbox parameters correct.

The Noise N code exists in the firmware but isn’t active for normal MQTT traffic. It might be used for OTA updates, or a provisioning step that only runs once, or it may be a remnant of an older protocol version. I don’t know. What matters is that in practice, the bridge encrypts and decrypts all messages with the same static 32-byte key stored in flash. Or at least mine does.

The Encryption Parameters

The bridge encrypts all MQTT payloads using LibHydrogen’s secretbox construction with a single symmetric key for both directions. That key lives at a fixed flash address (0x3f9010) and can be read without modifying the device.

The encryption parameters are straightforward:

  • Algorithm: hydro_secretbox (LibHydrogen)
  • Key: 32 bytes at flash address 0x3f9010
  • Context: the ASCII string 12345678
  • Message ID: 0 (constant for all messages)

Some might see these SecretBox context and message ID parameters and have a chuckle, but I don’t think Flume has done anything wrong in choosing them. The libhydrogen docs say about context that its purpose is to mitigate accidental bugs by separating domains. There’s probably only one domain in this scheme, so 12345678 is just as appropriate as any other context. And regarding message IDs, the docs also say

If this mechanism is not required by an application, using a constant msg_id such as 0 is also totally fine. Message identifiers are optional and do not have to be unique.

They were findable in the firmware, or guessable although clearly I didn’t guess them correctly last time. Regardless, with these parameters known, any message can be decrypted.

Reading the Key

The bridge’s ESP8266 has labeled UART pins on the board. By connecting a 3.3V USB-to-serial adapter and pulling GPIO0 low during power-on, the chip enters UART download mode. From there, esptool can read arbitrary flash regions:

esptool read_flash 0x3f9010 0x20 device_sk.bin
xxd -p -c 32 device_sk.bin

This prints a 64-character hex string, the device secret key. The bridge doesn’t need to be reflashed or modified in any way. Remove the GPIO0 jumper, reassemble, and the bridge boots normally.

The Relay Architecture

With the key and encryption parameters in hand, I built flumewatch, a transparent man-in-the-middle relay that sits between the bridge and Flume’s cloud server. It forwards all traffic untouched while decrypting a copy of each message for local consumption.

The bridge connects to mqtt.prod.flumetech.com on port 1883 (plain TCP, no TLS). By redirecting this traffic at the network layer, either with DNS overrides or destination NAT on the router, the bridge connects to the relay instead.

The relay is a Node.js process running an Aedes MQTT broker. When the bridge connects, the relay:

  1. Accepts the bridge’s MQTT CONNECT (capturing its client ID and credentials)
  2. Opens its own connection to mqtt.prod.flumetech.com using those same credentials
  3. Mirrors all subscriptions from the bridge to the upstream server
  4. Forwards every message in both directions, decrypting each payload for logging

Because the relay forwards encrypted payloads byte-for-byte, neither the bridge nor Flume’s server can tell anything has changed. The bridge continues its normal operation and the Flume mobile app works as usual.

I built libhydrogen-wasm, an Emscripten compilation of LibHydrogen to WebAssembly, specifically to handle the decryption in JavaScript.

What the Traffic Reveals

Messages travel on MQTT topics following the pattern 2/<type>/12/<device_id>/<counter>. The bridge subscribes to responses/<device_id>/# for each device (one for the bridge itself, one for the sensor) to receive downstream messages from Flume.

Connection Sequence

When the bridge powers on, the handshake tells a clear story:

Step 1: Identification (type 7). The bridge’s first message identifies itself with a firmware branch and commit:

{"bridge_id": null, "branch": "squidward", "sha_full": "2f1c870a72eca7d7eb38cb145718a202fe1c4a86"}

Step 2: Boot logs (type 3). Immediately after, the bridge sends diagnostic log messages with its reset reason and firmware version:

[
  {"timestamp": 0, "type": 1, "level": 4, "message": "RST REASON:  DIRTY  "},
  {"timestamp": 0, "type": 1, "level": 4, "message": "SDK reset #6: external"},
  {"timestamp": 0, "type": 1, "level": 4, "message": "SHA: 2f1c870a72eca7d7eb38cb145718a202fe1c4a86 | BRANCH: squidward"}
]

Step 3: Server response. Flume’s server acknowledges the connection, lists paired sensors, and returns a settings object:

{
  "code": 602,
  "message": "Request OK",
  "timestamp": 1785096108,
  "sensors": ["62AC1323E5A55F6F"],
  "devices": [{"uuid": "62AC1323E5A55F6F", "hardware_id": "ASY-00007"}],
  "settings": {
    "1": 1, "2": "/provisioning", "3": "/frames",
    "4": "/responses", "5": "mqtt.flumewater.com:1883",
    "6": 30000, "7": 1200000, "8": 4093, "9": 65281,
    "10": 14, "11": 261135, "12": 12, "13": 60, "14": 0
  }
}

The settings include the MQTT endpoint ("5": "mqtt.flumewater.com:1883", confirming plain TCP with no TLS), what appear to be timing intervals ("6": 30000, "7": 1200000 — possibly reporting cadence and heartbeat interval in milliseconds), and various configuration flags whose purposes are unknown.

Step 4: Post-handshake events (type 4). Once the handshake completes, the bridge fires a batch of event codes:

[
  {"timestamp": 1785096110, "type": 1},
  {"timestamp": 1785096110, "type": 1024},
  {"timestamp": 1785096110, "type": 16384}
]

The event codes are powers of 2. Their exact meanings are unknown, but they appear consistently after a successful handshake, suggesting they signal startup state transitions.

Water Flow Data

The most interesting messages are type 1, published on the sensor’s device topic. These contain timestamped values that increase monotonically:

[
  {"timestamp": 1785104646, "value": 3828906},
  {"timestamp": 1785104676, "value": 3828907},
  {"timestamp": 1785104691, "value": 3828908},
  {"timestamp": 1785104716, "value": 3828909},
  {"timestamp": 1785104731, "value": 3828910},
  {"timestamp": 1785104767, "value": 3828911}
]

The value field appears to be a cumulative counter, likely magnetometer pulses from the water meter’s rotating element, though that’s an inference based on the hardware. At times when water use is low, the counter increments by 1 every 15–30 seconds. At times when water use is higher, it increments faster:

[
  {"timestamp": 1785105201, "value": 3828929},
  {"timestamp": 1785105206, "value": 3828932},
  {"timestamp": 1785105211, "value": 3828936},
  {"timestamp": 1785105216, "value": 3828941},
  {"timestamp": 1785105221, "value": 3828943}
]

Here the counter jumps by 3–5 every 5 seconds. The relationship between counter increments and actual water volume is unknown; calibrating against a container of known volume would establish the conversion factor.

Sensor Status

Type 2 messages on the sensor topic carry a collection of bitmask-keyed fields:

[{
  "1": 2, "2": 17, "4": 18, "8": 7,
  "16": -79, "32": 3252, "128": 0,
  "1024": 24, "2048": 7, "4096": 0, "8192": 1,
  "16384": 3214, "131072": 3530, "262144": 50,
  "timestamp": 1785105287
}]

Some fields are identifiable by their value ranges:

Key Likely meaning Reasoning
16 RSSI (dBm) -79 is a typical radio signal strength
32 Battery (mV) 3252 → 3.252V, reasonable for lithium
16384 Reference voltage? 3214 mV, close to battery

Bridge Status

The bridge reports its own type 2 status less frequently:

[{"4": 28496, "32": -87, "128": 13, "256": 10, "512": -60, "timestamp": 1785105496}]
Key Likely meaning Reasoning
32 Sensor RSSI (dBm) -87, the 915 MHz radio link
512 WiFi RSSI (dBm) -60, typical for indoor WiFi
4 Uptime or free heap 28496, could be seconds or bytes

Heartbeats

Flume’s server sends periodic heartbeats (type 4, downstream) which the bridge echoes back verbatim as type 6:

{
  "timestamp": 1785105391038968,
  "heartbeat": {"id": "c4fc411648ca757e2f5210aa9af441f7", "seq": 1}
}

The timestamp appears to be microsecond-precision. The sequence number increments with each heartbeat; I’ve observed them arriving roughly every 10 minutes.

Wrapping Up

Since this time I have actually decrypted information on the network, I decided to be a responsible human and actually let the folks at Flume know what I’d done. They responded professionally and confirmed that each device has a random secret key, so nobody’s water usage info should be compromised by my publishing this blog entry.

James Fazio (Flume CTO) wanted to point out that

If the [bridge] device is configured to connect to a local MQTT server rather than Flume’s service, it will no longer receive firmware updates or technical support from Flume.

I probably will actually go back to using the Flume cloud MQTT service soon because I do want my device to have Flume’s support. I don’t think Flume can tell the difference between when I am or am not running my proxy. But it is possible because of all the blunt network shenanigans I pulled to redirect the traffic and that could indeed prevent firmware updates. Now at least we know that we can keep these devices running even without Flume should that need ever arise.

In my opinion, the security employed here is actually adequate. I was only able to gain access to this information because I had prolonged physical access to the hardware, a willingness to probe my device with esptool and complete access to the local network where it lives. That’s a pretty high bar, especially if anyone can learn the same info by opening my water meter pot on the sidewalk and having a look.

I know that by publishing, this all may get “fixed” in a security update. But I honestly hope it doesn’t. I would like to offer an idea for Flume.

How about a ‘developer mode’ where I can specify my own, or at least an additional MQTT server? It could make a best-effort delivery. It might even be useful for your own developers. And indicating that the feature is only for developers means it wouldn’t have to be a first class product feature with all the support burden that comes along for the ride. If that had existed, I definitely would not have spent all this time working on what turned out to be an interesting puzzle for me.

What More Could Be Done

The relay works and the data is flowing. Some open threads:

  • Pulse-to-volume calibration. Running a known volume of water while watching the counter will determine the conversion factor.
  • Local dashboarding. With decoded flow data available, piping it into InfluxDB or Home Assistant would provide local-only water monitoring independent of Flume’s cloud.
  • Bitmask field identification. Longer observation across different conditions (low battery, weak signal, temperature changes) should reveal what the remaining status fields encode.
  • Reporting cadence. Flow data arrives in batches roughly every 30 seconds. Flume’s handshake response may control this; a crafted response might increase resolution.

The full relay implementation is available at github.com/stevecrozz/flumewatch.

content_html_zh:
在我之前的文章中，我拆解了 Flume 水监测器，并追踪了它从传感器、通过桥接器直至 Flume 云 MQTT 服务器的通信路径。 我识别了加密库（LibHydrogen），提取了固件 ELF，甚至通过破坏闪存中的公钥来强制桥发送明文。 但这种做法具有破坏性。网桥无法完成与Flume服务器的握手，因此真实数据停止流动。

以为自己已经走进了死胡同，结果却发现了另一条路，这对我来说是很常见的事情。 我越来越多地想到我可以做些什么不同的事情，以及我可以做哪些进一步的研究。 因此，我开始继续追求我不健康的痴迷，即弄清楚如何在网络上读取这些数据。

为什么我认为这会更难

该固件包含完整的 LibHydrogen Noise N 密钥交换实现。 在反汇编中，Hydro_kx_n_1位于0x4023382c（客户端），flume_kx_init_client位于0x40234550，使用PSK=NULL和从闪存加载的服务器公钥来调用它。 这些函数对会话密钥存储位置具有真正的交叉引用。 一切都指向桥与 Flume 的服务器协商临时会话密钥，如果不将自定义密钥对写入闪存并在中继中实现完整的密钥交换，就不可能进行被动解密。 我确实这样做了，并希望看到它发挥作用，但又面临着又一次失望。

从之前的调查来看，当我使密钥存储区域上的 magic prefix 失效时，Flume 的服务器响应错误 174：“PHydro 加密密钥交换功能失败”。 该错误消息与固件中的密钥交换代码相结合，使人确信会话密钥正在发挥作用。

但是，当我实际捕获实时流量并尝试仅使用静态设备密钥进行解密时，所有内容都可以干净地解密。 不涉及会话密钥。 我确定我上次尝试过这个，但我一定没有让所有秘密盒参数正确。

Noise N 代码存在于固件中，但对于正常 MQTT 流量不活跃。 它可能用于 OTA 更新，或仅运行一次的配置步骤，也可能是旧协议版本的残余。 我不知道。 重要的是，在实践中，桥接器使用存储在闪存中的相同静态 32 字节密钥来加密和解密所有消息。 或者至少我的是这样。

加密参数

该桥使用 LibHydrogen 的秘密盒结构对所有 MQTT 有效负载进行加密，并在两个方向上使用单个对称密钥。 该密钥位于固定闪存地址 (0x3f9010)，无需修改设备即可读取。

加密参数很简单：

  • 算法： Hydro_secretbox (LibHydrogen)
  • 密钥：闪存地址 0x3f9010 处的 32 字节
  • 上下文：ASCII 字符串 12345678
  • 消息 ID：0（所有消息均不变）

有些人可能会看到这些 SecretBox 上下文和消息 ID 参数并轻笑，但我不认为 Flume 在选择它们时做错了什么。 libHydrogen 文档谈到上下文时说，其目的是通过分离域来减少意外错误。 此方案中可能只有一个域，因此 12345678 与任何其他上下文一样合适。 关于消息 ID，文档还说

如果应用程序不需要此机制，则使用常量 msg_id（例如 0）也完全可以。 消息标识符是可选的，并且不必是唯一的。

它们可以在固件中找到，或者可以猜测，尽管我上次显然没有猜对。 无论如何，只要知道这些参数，任何消息都可以被解密。

读取密钥

该桥的 ESP8266 在板上标有 UART 引脚。 通过连接 3.3V USB 转串口适配器并在上电期间将 GPIO0 拉低，芯片进入 UART 下载模式。 从那里，esptool 可以读取任意闪存区域：

esptool read_flash 0x3f9010 0x20 device_sk.bin
xxd -p -c 32 device_sk.bin

这将打印 64 个字符的十六进制字符串，即设备密钥。 这座桥不需要以任何方式重新闪光或修改。 移除GPIO0跳线，重新组装，桥接器正常启动。

中继架构

有了密钥和加密参数，我构建了 Flumewatch，这是一个位于网桥和 Flume 云服务器之间的透明中间人中继。 它原封不动地转发所有流量，同时解密每条消息的副本以供本地使用。

该网桥通过端口 1883 连接到 mqtt.prod.flumetech.com（纯 TCP，无 TLS）。 通过在网络层重定向此流量（使用路由器上的 DNS 覆盖或目标 NAT），网桥将连接到中继。

中继是一个运行 Aedes MQTT 代理的 Node.js 进程。 当桥连接时，继电器：

  1. 接受网桥的 MQTT CONNECT（捕获其客户端 ID 和凭据）
  2. 使用相同的凭据打开其自己的与 mqtt.prod.flumetech.com 的连接
  3. 将所有订阅从桥接器镜像到上游服务器
  4. 双向转发每条消息，解密每个有效负载以进行记录

由于中继逐字节转发加密的有效负载，因此桥接器和 Flume 的服务器都无法得知任何内容发生了变化。 桥梁继续正常运行，Flume 移动应用程序正常运行。

我构建了 libHydrogen-wasm，这是 LibHydrogen 到 WebAssembly 的 Emscripten 编译，专门用于处理 JavaScript 中的解密。

交通揭示了什么

消息按照 2/<type>/12/<device_id>/<counter> 模式在 MQTT 主题上传输。 桥接器订阅每个设备的response/<device_id>/#（一个用于桥接器本身，一个用于传感器）以接收来自Flume的下游消息。

连接顺序

当桥通电时，握手会讲述一个清晰的故事：

第 1 步：识别（类型 7）。 桥的第一条消息用固件分支和提交来标识自己：

{"bridge_id": null, "branch": "squidward", "sha_full": "2f1c870a72eca7d7eb38cb145718a202fe1c4a86"}

步骤 2：启动日志（类型 3）。 之后，网桥立即发送诊断日志消息及其重置原因和固件版本：

[
  {"timestamp": 0, "type": 1, "level": 4, "message": "RST REASON:  DIRTY  "},
  {"timestamp": 0, "type": 1, "level": 4, "message": "SDK reset #6: external"},
  {"timestamp": 0, "type": 1, "level": 4, "message": "SHA: 2f1c870a72eca7d7eb38cb145718a202fe1c4a86 | BRANCH: squidward"}
]

步骤3：服务器响应。 Flume 的服务器确认连接，列出配对的传感器，并返回一个设置对象：

{
  "code": 602,
  "message": "Request OK",
  "timestamp": 1785096108,
  "sensors": ["62AC1323E5A55F6F"],
  "devices": [{"uuid": "62AC1323E5A55F6F", "hardware_id": "ASY-00007"}],
  "settings": {
    "1": 1, "2": "/provisioning", "3": "/frames",
    "4": "/responses", "5": "mqtt.flumewater.com:1883",
    "6": 30000, "7": 1200000, "8": 4093, "9": 65281,
    "10": 14, "11": 261135, "12": 12, "13": 60, "14": 0
  }
}

这些设置包括 MQTT 端点（“5”：“mqtt.flumewater.com:1883”，确认没有 TLS 的普通 TCP）、时间间隔（“6”：30000、“7”：1200000 — 可能以毫秒为单位报告节奏和心跳间隔）以及各种用途未知的配置标志。

步骤 4：握手后事件（类型 4）。 握手完成后，网桥会触发一批事件代码：

[
  {"timestamp": 1785096110, "type": 1},
  {"timestamp": 1785096110, "type": 1024},
  {"timestamp": 1785096110, "type": 16384}
]

事件代码是 2 的幂。 它们的确切含义尚不清楚，但它们在成功握手后一致出现，表明它们表示启动状态转换。

水流数据

最有趣的消息是类型 1，发布在传感器的设备主题上。 它们包含单调增加的时间戳值：

[
  {"timestamp": 1785104646, "value": 3828906},
  {"timestamp": 1785104676, "value": 3828907},
  {"timestamp": 1785104691, "value": 3828908},
  {"timestamp": 1785104716, "value": 3828909},
  {"timestamp": 1785104731, "value": 3828910},
  {"timestamp": 1785104767, "value": 3828911}
]

值字段似乎是一个累积计数器，可能是来自水表旋转元件的磁力计脉冲，尽管这是基于硬件的推断。 当用水量较低时，计数器每 15-30 秒就会增加 1。 有时，用水量较高时，其增加速度会更快：

[
  {"timestamp": 1785105201, "value": 3828929},
  {"timestamp": 1785105206, "value": 3828932},
  {"timestamp": 1785105211, "value": 3828936},
  {"timestamp": 1785105216, "value": 3828941},
  {"timestamp": 1785105221, "value": 3828943}
]

这里计数器每 5 秒跳动 3-5 次。 计数器增量与实际水量之间的关系未知；根据已知体积的容器进行校准将建立转换系数。

传感器状态

传感器主题上的类型 2 消息携带位掩码键控字段的集合：

[{
  "1": 2, "2": 17, "4": 18, "8": 7,
  "16": -79, "32": 3252, "128": 0,
  "1024": 24, "2048": 7, "4096": 0, "8192": 1,
  "16384": 3214, "131072": 3530, "262144": 50,
  "timestamp": 1785105287
}]

某些字段可以通过其值范围来识别：

Key 可能的含义 推理
16 接收信号强度指示 (dBm) -79是典型的无线电信号强度
32 电池（毫伏） 3252 → 3.252V，对于锂电来说合理
16384 参考电压？ 3214 mV，靠近电池

网桥状态

网桥报告其自身 2 类状态的频率较低：

[{"4": 28496, "32": -87, "128": 13, "256": 10, "512": -60, "timestamp": 1785105496}]
Key 可能的含义 推理
32 传感器 RSSI (dBm) -87，915 MHz 无线电链路
512 WiFi RSSI (dBm) -60，室内 WiFi 的典型值
4 正常运行时间或空闲堆 28496，可以是秒或字节

心跳

Flume 的服务器发送周期性的心跳（类型 4，下游），桥接器将其逐字回显为类型 6：

{
  "timestamp": 1785105391038968,
  "heartbeat": {"id": "c4fc411648ca757e2f5210aa9af441f7", "seq": 1}
}

时间戳似乎是微秒精度的。 序列号随着每次心跳而递增；我观察到他们大约每 10 分钟到达一次。

总结

自从这次我真正解密了网络上的信息后，我决定做一个负责任的人，让 Flume 的人们知道我做了什么。 他们做出了专业的回应，并确认每个设备都有一个随机密钥，因此我发布此博客条目不应损害任何人的用水信息。

James Fazio（Flume 首席技术官）想要指出的是

如果[bridge]设备配置为连接到本地MQTT服务器而不是Flume的服务，它将不再接收来自Flume的固件更新或技术支持。

我可能很快就会重新使用 Flume 云 MQTT 服务，因为我确实希望我的设备得到 Flume 的支持。 我认为 Flume 无法区分我何时运行或不运行代理。 但这是可能的，因为我为了重定向流量而进行了所有生硬的网络恶作剧，这确实可能阻止固件更新。 现在至少我们知道，即使没有 Flume，我们也可以在需要时保持这些设备运行。

在我看来，这里采用的安全措施实际上是足够的。 我之所以能够访问这些信息，是因为我对硬件进行了长时间的物理访问，愿意使用 esptool 探测我的设备，并完全访问它所在的本地网络。 这是一个相当高的标准，特别是如果任何人都可以通过打开人行道上的水表壶看看来了解相同的信息。

我知道通过发布，这一切可能会在安全更新中得到“修复”。 但老实说我希望不会。 我想为 Flume 提供一个想法。

我可以指定自己的或至少一个额外的 MQTT 服务器的“开发者模式”怎么样？ 它可以尽力交付。 它甚至可能对您自己的开发人员有用。 并且表明该功能仅适用于开发人员意味着它不必是一流的产品功能，并且会带来所有支持负担。 如果存在的话，我绝对不会花这么多时间来研究这个对我来说很有趣的谜题。

还可以做些什么

继电器工作并且数据正在流动。 一些开放的线程：

  • 脉冲体积校准。 在观察计数器的同时运行已知体积的水将确定转换系数。
  • 本地仪表板。 有了解码后的流量数据，将其传输到 InfluxDB 或 Home Assistant 将提供独立于 Flume 云的仅限本地的水监控。
  • 位掩码字段标识。 对不同条件（电池电量低、信号弱、温度变化）进行更长时间的观察应该可以揭示剩余状态字段编码的内容。
  • 报告节奏。 流数据大约每 30 秒批量到达。 Flume 的握手响应可能会控制这一点；精心设计的响应可能会提高分辨率。

完整的中继实现可在 github.com/stevecrozz/flumewatch 上找到。
